practical.title: Your First C Program: Hello, World! — Personalized Greeting Lab
practical.sourceActivity: Your First C Program: Hello, World! — Personalized Greeting Lab

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the baseline greeting.c
tasks.narratorGuide: Warm welcome! In this first short task you'll open and run a complete C program named greeting.c. Notice the role of #include <stdio.h> (it provides printf), the main function (program entry), the printf call (prints text), the escape sequence \n (newline), and return 0 (signals success). We'll compile with clang and run the produced executable. Understanding this baseline output will make the effects of later edits obvious. After running, pay attention to exactly what prints and whether the prompt returns on the next line — that detail is important for later experiments.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Personalize the greeting
tasks.narratorGuide: Great — now you'll make a focused change. Replace the string inside printf with a personalized message such as "Hello, Cohortia Learner!\n" or your own name. This is intentionally one small edit so you can recompile quickly and observe the effect. After compiling and running, try removing the \n and running again to see how the terminal prompt behaves. We'll also observe that recompiling is necessary for changes to take effect; editing without recompiling won't change program output.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Multiple printfs and reading compiler errors
tasks.narratorGuide: Now we'll extend the program safely. Add a second printf to demonstrate how multiple calls behave and how the newline affects output flow. Next, intentionally remove a semicolon to provoke a compilation error — this is purposeful practice: compiler errors are not scary when you approach them as diagnostic messages. Read the error, notice the line number and suggestion, then fix the code and recompile. This sequence helps you learn to iterate: write small changes, compile, read messages, fix, repeat.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Use a variable and format specifier
tasks.narratorGuide: For the final task, convert the hard-coded literal into a char array variable and use printf with a format specifier (%s) to print it. This demonstrates how formatted output works and how you can separate data from presentation. It's a minimal change but it opens the door to dynamic content: later you'll read user input into a buffer and print it the same way. After compiling and running, verify the output matches the variable contents. If it does, you've successfully integrated data and formatting.

safety.learnerWarning: This practical runs in an isolated workspace. Do not use real credentials or production resources.

cleanup.instructions: Discard the isolated workspace after completion.
